answer.rationale: With the line running at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, delivery continuity is the binding constraint, and the contract lapses in 14 days with no auto-renew, ruling out defer_decision. Switching to a low-cost vendor (memory_c2) offers cost savings but introduces onboarding/integration risk that this environment cannot absorb, so it's deprioritized despite the 18% cut mandate. Renegotiating with the incumbent (memory_c4, memory_c6) has a track record of recovering real margin and unlocking volume pricing without disrupting integration or service scope (memory_c1 corroborates stability), making it the best fit for minimizing TCO without raising delivery risk. I verified c4 and c6 since they carry the specific quantitative claims (margin recovery, volume-pricing cost cuts) the decision leans on most heavily; c1 is used as secondary corroboration but not independently verified this cycle. Flagging downstream risk: negotiated terms may not fully close the 18% gap, and a second-source evaluation (memory_c3) for the constrained component still needs attention next cycle to address single-point-of-failure exposure.
